Ragas is a framework that automatically evaluates Retrieval‑Augmented Generation pipelines without needing reference answers.
It supplies a suite of metrics to judge how well the retriever finds relevant passages, how faithfully the LLM uses them, and the overall quality of the generated output.
The framework targets fast, reference‑free assessment, offering proxies for correctness and passage usefulness, and integrates with common RAG toolkits such as llama‑index and Langchain.

Ragas tackles the need for reference‑free evaluation of RAG pipelines, providing metrics that assess retrieval relevance, passage usefulness, and generation faithfulness without requiring ground‑truth human annotations【1】.
It enables automated assessment of correctness proxies and retrieval quality when reference answers are unavailable【2】.

CARROT uses a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) based strategy to search for the optimal chunk‑combination order within the cost constraint【2】.
It applies MCTS to explore and select the best combination of chunks for retrieval‑augmented generation【1】.
CARROT yields roughly a 30 % performance gain over baseline models, as shown by the experimental results.
IGMiRAG improves over the state‑of‑the‑art baseline by 4.8 % in Exact Match (EM) and 5.0 % in F1 overall【1】.
IGMiRAG first parses the query with a Retrieval‑Strategy Parser (question parser) that extracts intuitive strategies from the user’s question【1】.
The extracted strategies are used to set how many hops of deductive pathways to follow, thereby controlling the mining depth【2】.
The same strategies also define the size of the memory window that will be examined, limiting or expanding the set of memories retrieved for the query【1】.
This dynamic adjustment enables adaptive deep mining that matches the complexity of each query【2】.
DDRO improves MRR@10 on the MS MARCO document benchmark by 7.4%
DDRO directly optimizes GenIR models with pairwise ranking supervision, aligning token‑level docid generation to document‑level relevance without any reward model or reinforcement step.

In contrast, RLRF relies on reinforcement learning: it first builds an auxiliary reward function from relevance feedback and then fine‑tunes the model with reinforcement learning, adding complexity and instability.
DDRO’s optimization is a single, supervised step, while RLRF requires a two‑stage process (reward modeling + RL) that is computationally expensive.
DDRO therefore eliminates the need for explicit reward modeling and reinforcement fine‑tuning, simplifying the training pipeline compared to RLRF.
